questions.q: The Makkans had rebuilt the Kabah smaller than Abraham’s original, and the Prophet left it so. What principle does the editorial draw from this?
options: Smaller buildings are always better
Not quite. The article says: Plan on the basis of what remains, rather than spend time recovering what was lost.
Plan on the basis of what remains, rather than spend time recovering what was lost
Yes. It could be used at once, just as it was.
Advice from others should be ignored
Not quite. The article says: Plan on the basis of what remains, rather than spend time recovering what was lost.
Old buildings should never be altered
Not quite. The article says: Plan on the basis of what remains, rather than spend time recovering what was lost.
questions.rationale: “The Prophet letting the Kabah continue in its square shape was an example of re-planning on the basis of what was already there.”

questions.q: Why does the editorial call differences of opinion “beautiful”?
options: They open the way to dialogue, which triggers new ideas and intellectual growth
Right. As the falling apple set Newton thinking.
They make life more entertaining
Not quite. The article says: They open the way to dialogue, which triggers new ideas and intellectual growth.
They keep people at a safe distance
Not quite. The article says: They open the way to dialogue, which triggers new ideas and intellectual growth.
They show who is right and who is wrong
Not quite. The article says: They open the way to dialogue, which triggers new ideas and intellectual growth.
questions.rationale: “If there are differences of opinion among people, it paves the way for dialogue. This dialogue becomes the stepping-stone to new thoughts and ideas.”

questions.article: The Arabs and the Emergence of Islam
questions.q: Who were the people known as Hanif among the ancient Arabs?
options: Truth-seekers who wished to worship God rightly and readily answered the Prophet’s call
Well read. “O God, I do not know how You should be worshipped.”
Guardians of the oases
Not quite. The article says: Truth-seekers who wished to worship God rightly and readily answered the Prophet’s call.
Poets of the desert tribes
Not quite. The article says: Truth-seekers who wished to worship God rightly and readily answered the Prophet’s call.
Traders who led the caravans
Not quite. The article says: Truth-seekers who wished to worship God rightly and readily answered the Prophet’s call.
questions.rationale: “These people were truth seekers… These people, true in nature took no time in responding to the call of Prophet Muhammad.”

questions.article: The Arabs and the Emergence of Islam
questions.q: How, according to the article, did the hard and simple life of the desert shape its people?
options: It left them without any moral code
Not quite. The article says: It made them realists with qualities such as truthfulness, keeping promises, courage and hospitality.
It made them realists with qualities such as truthfulness, keeping promises, courage and hospitality
Yes. Nature was their school.
It made them distrust all strangers
Not quite. The article says: It made them realists with qualities such as truthfulness, keeping promises, courage and hospitality.
It made them fond of luxury
Not quite. The article says: It made them realists with qualities such as truthfulness, keeping promises, courage and hospitality.
questions.rationale: “This extremely simple, austere life made them realists. All this was responsible for producing in them the qualities which the Arabs called manliness.”

questions.q: Which three words does the article say people find hardest of all to utter?
options: “I am sorry”
Not quite. The article says: “I am wrong”.
“I need help”
Not quite. The article says: “I am wrong”.
“I am wrong”
Correct. Self-love resists admitting a mistake.
“I forgive you”
Not quite. The article says: “I am wrong”.
questions.rationale: “To utter the three damning words, ‘I am wrong’ is so difficult that in the long history of humankind there have been very few cases of people who have actually brought themselves to utter them.”

questions.q: What “secular aspect” does the article find in belief in the oneness of God?
options: It reduces the need for study
Not quite. The article says: It builds the habit of concentration – an integrated mind directed to a single point.
It improves physical health
Not quite. The article says: It builds the habit of concentration – an integrated mind directed to a single point.
It increases one’s wealth
Not quite. The article says: It builds the habit of concentration – an integrated mind directed to a single point.
It builds the habit of concentration – an integrated mind directed to a single point
Right. The opposite of a “grasshopper” mind.
questions.rationale: “When a believer adopts the belief that God is only one, he develops the habit of concentration… Thus tawhid leads to focused thinking.”

questions.q: A pinch of dye colours a whole glass of water. What does this illustrate in the article?
options: One person can mislead a crowd
Not quite. The article says: Love for the Creator naturally spreads into love for all people.
Love for the Creator naturally spreads into love for all people
Well reasoned. Love has a practical, social side.
Feelings fade when mixed with duties
Not quite. The article says: Love for the Creator naturally spreads into love for all people.
A small mistake spoils a whole life
Not quite. The article says: Love for the Creator naturally spreads into love for all people.
questions.rationale: “When a person has love in his heart for his Creator, at the same time he cannot resist showing his love to his neighbours.”

questions.q: Two men brought the Prophet an inheritance dispute with no witnesses. When he warned that taking another’s due would be like accepting a firebrand, what did they do?
options: They asked for another judge
Not quite. The article says: Each wept and offered his own share to the other.
Both withdrew and never spoke again
Not quite. The article says: Each wept and offered his own share to the other.
Each demanded that the other swear an oath
Not quite. The article says: Each wept and offered his own share to the other.
Each wept and offered his own share to the other
Yes. He then told them to divide it fairly and draw lots.
questions.rationale: “At these words, both the Ansar broke down and wept. ‘Prophet of God!’ they both cried out, ‘he can have my rightful share!’”

questions.q: Someone addressed Abdullah ibn Umar as “most noble of men, son of the most noble.” How did he reply?
options: He rejected the praise: he was just one of God’s servants, and such praise destroys a man
Exactly. Humility in the face of flattery.
He thanked the man warmly
Not quite. The article says: He rejected the praise: he was just one of God’s servants, and such praise destroys a man.
He kept silent and smiled
Not quite. The article says: He rejected the praise: he was just one of God’s servants, and such praise destroys a man.
He returned an equal compliment
Not quite. The article says: He rejected the praise: he was just one of God’s servants, and such praise destroys a man.
questions.rationale: “I am just one of God’s servants; in Him do I have hope, and Him do I fear. By God, you are bent on destroying a man with such praise.”

questions.article: The Way of Balance and Moderation
questions.q: To which sphere does the article say the way of moderation applies?
options: Neither practice nor belief
Not quite. The article says: Practical dealings with others, so as to live in harmony – not matters of belief and principle.
Only matters of food and dress
Not quite. The article says: Practical dealings with others, so as to live in harmony – not matters of belief and principle.
Practical dealings with others, so as to live in harmony – not matters of belief and principle
Right. In principle, the ideal is always sought.
Religious beliefs above all
Not quite. The article says: Practical dealings with others, so as to live in harmony – not matters of belief and principle.
questions.rationale: “Balance is required in practical matters and not in religious beliefs or principles.”
